We start by noting two facts about the food‐suggestions made by the students:

• 218 students said “mashed potatoes and bacon.”
• 351 students said “bacon only.”

A useful first step is to add the two numbers to see how many students overall wanted bacon. (In fact,
  218 + 351 = 569.)

Now, if you look at the “mashed potatoes‐bacon” and “bacon only” groups you get a “two‐part” breakup of 569. In other words, out of 569 bacon‐supporters the two groups are 218 and 351. Notice that

  351 ÷ 569 ≈ 0.617   and  218 ÷ 569 ≈ 0.382.

These percentages are very nearly the “golden‐section” numbers (≈61.8% and 38.2%) that occur when a whole is divided into two parts. (Indeed, one of the golden‐section properties is that the ratio of the larger part to the whole is the same as the ratio of the whole to the larger part – here 351/569 ≈ 0.617 and 569/351 ≈ 1.618; the number 1.618 is often called the golden mean.)

But there is a second—and in this puzzle the intended—key step. Look at the two numbers:
  351 (bacon‐only supporters) and 218 (mashed potatoes plus bacon supporters).

If you subtract the smaller number from the larger you get

  351 – 218 = 133.

It turns out that many “riddle‐style” puzzles (especially ones that have the final, “extra‐thematic” question such as “How deep was the water?”) are solved by interpreting the numbers in a hidden way and then “reading” the answer off from a simple arithmetic operation—here the difference 351 minus 218.

Thus, by following both the idea of the impressive golden‐section proportions (a typical “delectable” puzzle device) and the simple arithmetic (351 – 218 = 133) one is led to the answer:

  \boxed{133}.

So, “How deep was the water?” is answered by 133.

  S = number sold.
